title: Cucumber, Gherkin Reference
text:
## Purpose of Gherkin
Gherkin is a business readable, domain specific language that lets you describe software behaviour without detailing how that behaviour is implemented. Gherkin serves two purposes: documentation and automated tests. Each Gherkin scenario is an executable specification of the system, written in plain language so business stakeholders, analysts, and developers share one description of behaviour.

## Given, When, Then
Given steps establish the initial context: they put the system in a known state before the user or external system starts interacting with it. Givens are the preconditions of the scenario, for example that a game has started or that a user is logged in. Avoid talking about user interaction in Givens; the Given is state, not action.
When steps describe an event or an action. This can be a person interacting with the system, or an event triggered by another system, for example guessing a word, inviting a friend, or withdrawing money.
Then steps describe an expected outcome, or result. The assertion should compare an observable output of the system (a report, a user interface, a message) against what is expected, not against something deeply internal that a user cannot see.

## And, But
Use And and But when you have several Givens, Whens, or Thens in a row. Instead of writing Given repeatedly, subsequent lines of the same type read And or But so the scenario flows naturally.

## Structure keywords
Feature: begins the file and groups related scenarios with a high level description. Rule (Gherkin 6+) groups scenarios that illustrate a single business rule. Scenario (or its synonym Example) is a concrete example that illustrates a business rule, following the pattern context, event, outcome. Background contains Given steps run before each scenario in the file, to avoid repeating the same context. Scenario Outline runs the same scenario multiple times with different values supplied by an Examples table, using placeholders written in angle brackets. Step arguments can be Doc Strings (large text passed with triple quotes) or Data Tables (pipe delimited rows).

## Example scenario
Given Mickey and Minnie have started a game / When Mickey guesses a word / Then Minnie sees that the guessed word was wrong. This shape, a known state, a single event, and an observable outcome, is the core discipline of acceptance criteria written in Gherkin.

title: Agile Alliance, INVEST (user story quality checklist)
text:
## INVEST
INVEST is a checklist to quickly evaluate the quality of a user story. If the story fails to meet one of these criteria, the team may want to reword it, or even reconsider it. The acronym stands for Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, and Testable.

## The six criteria
Independent (of all others): a story should be self contained so it can be scheduled and implemented in any order, avoiding hidden dependencies on other stories.
Negotiable (not a specific contract for features): a story is not a detailed specification; it is a reminder of a conversation. The details are negotiated between the team and the customer, not frozen up front.
Valuable (or vertical): a story must deliver value to the stakeholders, and ideally cut vertically through the system (a thin end to end slice) rather than being a horizontal technical layer with no standalone value.
Estimable (to a good approximation): the team must be able to estimate the size of the story. Inability to estimate usually signals the story is too big, too vague, or lacks domain knowledge.
Small (so as to fit within an iteration): a good story is small enough to be completed comfortably within one iteration; large stories (epics) should be split.
Testable (in principle, even if there isn't a test for it yet): you must be able to write a test that proves the story is done. An untestable story is usually a sign that the acceptance criteria are unclear.

## Origin
The INVEST acronym was created in 2003 by Bill Wake in an article on XP123, and was popularized in Mike Cohn's 2004 book User Stories Applied, which discusses these criteria in depth. INVEST is a heuristic, not a hard gate: it is a lens for spotting stories that will cause trouble later.

title: Karl Wiegers, Writing Good Requirements (Software Development, May 1999)
text:
## Characteristics of excellent requirement statements
Karl Wiegers lists the properties every individual requirement should have.
Correct: each requirement must accurately describe the functionality to be delivered, and it must match its source (a use case, a system requirement, a customer voice). The customer representatives are the ones who can judge correctness.
Feasible: it must be possible to implement each requirement within the known capabilities and limitations of the system and its environment. To avoid infeasible requirements, have a developer work with analysts throughout elicitation.
Necessary: each requirement should document something the customers really need, or something required for conformance to an external interface, standard, or regulation. Every requirement should originate from a source that has the authority to specify requirements.
Prioritized: assign an implementation priority to each requirement, feature, or use case, indicating how essential it is to a particular release. A common scheme uses high (must be included), medium (can be deferred), and low (nice to have).
Unambiguous: the reader of a requirement statement should be able to draw only one interpretation of it. Write requirements in the simple, direct, straightforward language of the user domain, not in convoluted phrasing.
Verifiable: you should be able to devise tests or use other verification approaches, such as inspection or demonstration, to check whether the requirement was properly implemented. Requirements that are not consistent, feasible, or unambiguous are also not verifiable.

## Characteristics of an excellent requirements specification
Complete: no requirements or necessary information are missing. Missing requirements are hard to spot because they are not there; organizing requirements hierarchically helps reviewers notice gaps. Use TBD (to be determined) as a standard flag for known missing information.
Consistent: consistent requirements do not conflict with other requirements in the same document or with higher level (system or business) requirements.
Modifiable: you must be able to revise the specification when necessary and maintain a history of changes to each requirement. This requires each requirement to be uniquely labeled and expressed separately from others so it can be referred to unambiguously.
Traceable: you should be able to link each requirement backward to its source and forward to the design elements, code, and tests that implement and verify it. Traceable requirements are uniquely labeled and written in a structured, fine grained way rather than in long narrative paragraphs.

## Words to avoid
Watch for ambiguous, subjective words that feel meaningful but cannot be verified: user friendly, easy, simple, rapid, efficient, several, state of the art, improved, maximize, and minimize. Also beware weak phrases and loopholes such as and/or, etc., and shall be able to support, which quietly widen scope. Replace them with measurable, testable statements.

title: Modern Analyst, An Overview of Requirements Elicitation
text:
## What elicitation is
Elicitation is the work of drawing out requirements that reside in the minds of stakeholders and in feedback that has not yet been obtained from end users. The approach must be logical and meticulous. Mistakes made in elicitation have repeatedly been shown to be major causes of system failure, so the goal is to thoroughly identify the business needs, risks, and assumptions of a project.

## Preparing to elicit
Understand the business need first: a comprehensive understanding of the true need prevents scope creep and gold plating and lets you pick the right stakeholders and the right techniques. Secure the appropriate stakeholders: BABOK stresses that analysts must actively engage stakeholders in defining requirements. Typical stakeholders include customers and end users, suppliers, project managers, quality analysts, regulators, sponsors, operational support, and subject matter experts. Schedule elicitation activities well in advance.

## Nine elicitation techniques
Brainstorming: gather stakeholders to produce numerous new ideas and derive themes for further analysis; a facilitator keeps focus on the business need and records every idea. Useful when existing solutions seem inadequate.
Document analysis: review existing documentation such as business plans, market studies, contracts, requests for proposal, statements of work, memos, guidelines, procedures, and training guides. Valuable when updating an existing system, but rarely sufficient on its own.
Focus groups: assemble pre qualified stakeholders to discuss needs and solutions; efficient for gathering a lot of information, helpful when key stakeholders lack imagination.
Interface analysis: examine how users interact with an application, or how applications interact with each other, describing the interface's purpose and content.
Interviews: one on one discussions that explore a stakeholder's perspective in depth. Research shows interviews are the most effective way of eliciting requirements. They may be structured or unstructured; share notes afterward to prevent misunderstanding.
Observation (job shadowing): passive observation (watch without interrupting) or active observation (ask questions throughout). Beneficial when the project will modify or enhance a current process.
Prototyping: build storyboards, navigation flows, paper prototypes, or screen flows so stakeholders can concretely identify, describe, and validate their interface needs; iterative.
Requirements workshops: structured, facilitated sessions of set duration to elicit, refine, and edit requirements, with a facilitator directing and a scribe recording, enabling immediate feedback.
Survey or questionnaire: gather data from a large group using closed (finite choice) or open ended questions; inexpensive, works when the population is large enough and the issues are clear enough, and the wording must be unambiguous.

title: Martin Fowler, GivenWhenThen
text:
## Given-When-Then
Given-When-Then is a style of representing tests, or any executable specification, using a specific format. It was developed by Daniel Terhorst-North and Chris Matts as part of Behavior-Driven Development (BDD). It appears as a structuring approach for many testing frameworks such as Cucumber, and it also works well as a way of thinking about how a scenario should be written.

## The three parts
The scenario is broken into three sections. Given describes the state of the world before you begin the behavior you are specifying: the pre-conditions of the test. When is the behavior that you are specifying: the single action under test. Then describes the changes you expect as a result of the specified behavior: the expected outcomes. You start with the Given clauses to set up the context, apply the single When to trigger the behavior, and check the Then clauses for the result.

## And
It is common to see ands used to combine multiple expressions within each clause, so a scenario may have several Given ... And ... lines and several Then ... And ... lines while keeping a single When.

## Example
Feature: User trades stocks. Scenario: User requests a sell before close of trading. Given I have 100 shares of MSFT stock, And I have 150 shares of APPL stock, And the time is before close of trading. When I ask to sell 20 shares of MSFT stock. Then I should have 80 shares of MSFT stock, And I should have 150 shares of APPL stock, And a sell order for 20 shares of MSFT stock should have been executed.

## Relationship to Arrange, Act, Assert
Given-When-Then is a reframing of the Arrange, Act, Assert pattern that Bill Wake introduced for unit tests. Given corresponds to Arrange, When to Act, and Then to Assert. The value of Given-When-Then is that it pushes you to separate setup, action, and verification, which keeps a scenario focused on one behavior at a time.

title: Agile Business Consortium (DSDM), What is MoSCoW Prioritization
text:
## MoSCoW
MoSCoW is a prioritization technique from the DSDM agile framework. The letters stand for Must have, Should have, Could have, and Won't have this time. The o's are added only to make the word pronounceable.

## The four categories
Must have: the Minimum Usable SubseT (MUST) of requirements that the project guarantees to deliver. The test for a Must have is: if it is not delivered, is the delivery worthless. If there is some way around it, even a manual and painful workaround, then it is a Should have or a Could have, not a Must have.
Should have: important but not vital. It may be painful to leave out, but the solution is still viable. A Should have may need a workaround but the delivered solution still works.
Could have: wanted or desirable but less important. It has less impact if left out compared with a Should have. Could haves are the first work to be dropped when time runs short.
Won't have this time: requirements the team has agreed will not be delivered in this timeframe. Recording them explicitly manages expectations and keeps them out of scope for now, without losing them forever.

## Allocating effort
MoSCoW prioritization is done on effort, not on a count of requirements. DSDM recommends no more than 60 percent Must have effort on a project, and a sensible pool of Could haves, typically around 20 percent of effort. Anything other than a Must have is, to some degree, contingency: the Shoulds and Coulds are the buffer that protects the deadline. If Must haves exceed about 60 percent of effort, the project's predictability and success are at risk, unless the environment, technology, and team are all well understood and external risks are minimal. This is why MoSCoW protects a fixed deadline: you flex scope (drop Coulds, then Shoulds) rather than moving the date.

title: Camunda, BPMN 2.0 Symbol Reference
text:
## BPMN 2.0 element categories
BPMN 2.0 (Business Process Model and Notation, maintained by the OMG) models a process as a flow of activities, events, and gateways connected by sequence flows, organized into pools and lanes.

## Activities and tasks
A task is an atomic activity. Task types include undefined, manual, user, receive, send, script, service, and business rule. Task markers include Loop (repeats until a condition applies), Multiple Instance (executes repeatedly in sequence or parallel), and Compensation. A Subprocess encapsulates complexity and is drawn with a plus sign; it can be embedded or global. A Call Activity is a globally reusable subprocess drawn with a thicker border. An Ad hoc subprocess holds activities that can be executed in any order, several times, or skipped. An Event subprocess is triggered by a start event and can be interrupting (continuous line) or non interrupting (dashed line).

## Gateways
Gateways control divergence and convergence of the flow. Exclusive (XOR): routes through exactly one path based on mutually exclusive conditions (data based). Parallel (AND): splits into paths executed simultaneously and merges by synchronizing them. Inclusive (OR): may take multiple paths depending on which conditions are met. Event based: routes based on which event happens next rather than on data.

## Events
Events are classified by position and by type. By position: Start (initiates the process), Intermediate (occurs during execution, and can be attached to an activity boundary), and End (concludes a path). By behavior: Catching events react to a defined trigger; Throwing events fire the trigger themselves; Non interrupting events (dashed border) can occur many times without stopping the activity. Specific triggers include None, Message (envelope), Timer (clock), Error (flash), Conditional, Signal (triangle), Link, Compensation, Escalation, Cancel, Multiple, and Parallel.

## Flows, pools, lanes, and data
Sequence Flow connects activities within the same pool or lane and defines execution order. Message Flow shows communication between participants and crosses pool boundaries. A Pool represents a participant or process and orchestrates its own tasks; Lanes subdivide a pool to assign responsibility to positions, roles, departments, or IT applications (this is swimlane modeling). A Data Object represents information flowing through the process, and a Data Store is a repository accessible across activities.

title: Mike Cohn (Mountain Goat Software), User Stories
text:
## What a user story is
A user story is a short description of desired functionality told from the perspective of someone who wants or needs that functionality. The written story is a reminder to have a conversation; the full requirement emerges through the conversation that follows. Stories deliberately defer some detail until the team is closer to doing the work, rather than capturing everything up front.

## The template
The standard form is: As a [type of user], I [need or want or am required] to [do something], so that [reason or benefit]. Example: As a conference attendee, I need to filter sessions by topic so that I can quickly find the sessions most relevant to me. The so that clause forces the story to name the value, which keeps teams from building features nobody needs.

## The three C's
Ron Jeffries described a story as three parts. Card: the short written description, once a physical card or sticky note, today a backlog item in a tool. Conversation: where understanding grows; the team discusses user goals, tradeoffs, edge cases, business rules, design options, and implementation concerns. Confirmation: how the team knows the story is complete, expressed as acceptance criteria, examples, tests, sketches, rules, or notes that clarify what must be true when the story is done.

## Epics and acceptance criteria
An epic is a large story, useful when the team wants to remember an important capability before knowing all the details; epics are later split into smaller stories. Acceptance criteria are details that help the team understand whether a story has been completed correctly, and may take the form of examples, rules, tests, or brief notes. Writing the confirmation before development starts is what makes a story testable in the INVEST sense.

title: Leaders Loop, Stakeholder Mapping and Analysis (Power/Interest Grid)
text:
## The power/interest grid
Stakeholder mapping plots each stakeholder on two axes. Power is the ability to shape outcomes through budget, authority, veto, expertise, or informal influence. Interest is how much the person cares about the initiative or outcome. This is the Mendelow power/interest grid, a foundational stakeholder analysis technique in business analysis.

## The four quadrants
Players (high power, high interest): Manage closely, through regular, intensive engagement such as weekly working sessions. These are the decision makers and key influencers.
Context setters (high power, low interest): Keep satisfied, with brief, infrequent updates that ensure no surprises. They can derail or radically change an initiative even though their day to day interest is low, so do not overburden them with detail but never blindside them.
Subjects (low power, high interest): Keep informed with structured communication beyond basic notification. They care and can be valuable allies even if they cannot directly drive outcomes.
Crowd (low power, low interest): Monitor with minimal active effort, watching for shifts in power or urgency.

## The mapping process
List everyone who can affect or is affected by the change. Place each person on the power by interest axes. Select the appropriate engagement posture per quadrant. Assess whether any legitimate or urgent claims are hidden in low power groups. Act, then re map when situations shift.

## Key caution
Do not dismiss low power, low interest stakeholders as permanently insignificant: legitimacy and urgency can emerge rapidly, and a Crowd stakeholder can move into another quadrant overnight. Stakeholder analysis is not a one time exercise; re map as the project and the political landscape change.

title: binaryphile, Cockburn Use Cases Guide
text:
## What a use case is
Following Alistair Cockburn, a use case captures what the system actually does, in a form that survives implementation changes. It documents the interactions between actors and a system under design (SUD) to achieve a measurable goal. The SUD is the boundary: the black box whose behavior is being documented.

## Actors and scope
The Primary Actor is the role that initiates the use case to achieve a goal. Secondary (supporting) actors are external systems the SUD calls upon. Scope names what is inside the black box versus outside it.

## Goal levels
Cockburn organizes use cases by three goal levels. Summary (Kite): encompasses multiple user goals and takes hours. User Goal (Sea Level): passes the Boss test, work a person could do in one sitting; typically 3 to 9 steps completed in minutes; ask can the primary actor go away happy after doing this. Subfunction (Fish): supports a user goal use case but lacks independent value, operating in seconds. Levels are drawn with a kite (above sea level), a wave (sea level), and a fish (below sea level).

## The template fields
Preconditions: assumed true, not tested; state only what is worth telling the reader. Minimal Guarantee: the promise to all stakeholders even when the use case fails, for example that an audit trail is preserved. Success Guarantee (postcondition): what must be true on successful completion, meeting all stakeholder interests. Trigger: the event that starts the use case.

## Main success scenario and extensions
The Main Success Scenario is the happy path: the numbered sequence in which the actor achieves the goal through interactions, validations, and state changes. Extensions are alternate paths keyed to the step number they branch from (for example 3a), and each extension ends by rejoining the main scenario, reaching a separate success, or ending in failure. Writing extensions is where a BA captures the real business rules and failure handling that a bare user story would miss.

title: Jeff Patton, The New Backlog (User Story Mapping)
text:
## The problem with a flat backlog
A prioritized flat backlog strips stories out of their organizational context, reducing a coherent system to what Jeff Patton calls a bag of context free mulch. You lose the big picture, the ability to see the whole, and the ability to plan a coherent release.

## The backbone
The story map restores context. At the top of the map are big stories that Patton calls user activities: large, essential capabilities arranged horizontally left to right in narrative flow. The order you would explain the behavior of the system in is the correct order. This row is the backbone, the essential spine of the system.

## The ribs and vertical priority
Beneath each activity hang smaller stories, the user tasks, the discrete steps users perform. These are arranged vertically, top to bottom, by priority. So the map has two dimensions at once: left to right is narrative flow (what the user does across the whole system), and top to bottom is priority (how essential each detail is).

## The walking skeleton
The stories highest on the map form the walking skeleton: the smallest possible system you could build that would give you end to end functionality. Slicing the map horizontally lets you carve out a first release that does something useful all the way through, then add depth in later increments, rather than building one activity fully while others are missing.

## Why mapping works
Mapping fixes three failures of the flat list: it preserves context, it reveals overlooked steps when you walk the map with stakeholders, and it makes release planning a matter of drawing horizontal slices that each deliver coherent, complete functionality. This is how a BA turns a pile of stories into a plan a stakeholder can actually see and agree to.

title: Wikipedia, Gold plating (software engineering) [anti-pattern]
text:
## Gold plating (anti-pattern)
Gold plating is the phenomenon of working on a project or task past the point of diminishing returns. It occurs when a manager or developer keeps enhancing a product beyond its original requirements, adding features the customer did not request, thinking the customer will be delighted to see additional or more polished features beyond what was asked for or expected.

## Why it is harmful
Gold plating is poor practice because it introduces unplanned risk: additional testing, extra documentation burden, cost overruns, and timeline delays, all for functionality nobody validated as needed. It violates frameworks like PMBOK and PRINCE2, which require adherence to the agreed scope. Best case, the customer accepts the extra work but forms unrealistically elevated expectations for future projects; worst case, the customer rejects the deliverable and the contract is jeopardized.

## Gold plating versus scope creep
Both involve unplanned work, but they differ in origin. Gold plating is voluntary enhancement by the delivery team beyond the requirements. Scope creep is uncontrolled expansion of the project boundary driven by external requests or changes. For a business analyst, the lesson is that every added feature must trace to a validated need; unrequested polish is a defect, not a gift. A requirement that no stakeholder asked for and that delivers no measured value should be cut, not built.

title: Scott Ambler, Examining the Big Requirements Up Front (BRUF) Approach [anti-pattern]
text:
## Big Requirements Up Front (anti-pattern)
BRUF is the traditional approach where requirements are defined and documented in detail early in the initiative, then handed to developers, with change management acting as a gatekeeper to minimize scope creep. Scott Ambler argues that a large, detailed requirements document written up front is one of the most wasteful practices in software.

## The wastage evidence
Ambler cites the Standish Group Chaos Report finding that on successful projects, 45 percent of the delivered functionality was never used and a further 19 percent was rarely used, which is roughly two thirds wastage. A big up front specification bakes this waste in.

## Why BRUF fails
Requirements change: months or years pass between finalizing the spec and deploying, during which market conditions, legislation, and strategy shift. Understanding evolves: what looks like changed requirements is often improved comprehension, because people are poor at predicting their needs but excellent at giving feedback once they see working software. Speculative requirements: when you ask stakeholders to brainstorm every possible future need up front, you guarantee unnecessary functionality. Artificial caps: teams negotiate the spec downward as resources dwindle, so the original detail was never real.

## The alternative
Ambler advocates high level requirements envisioning taking several days up to a maximum of two weeks, then just in time detail through short model storming sessions of five to ten minutes, prioritized iterative delivery that lets stakeholders control scope, budget, and schedule, and continuous feedback loops. The BA lesson: specify at the last responsible moment and let working software, not a frozen document, drive the detail. A big document nobody reads is not requirements; it is inventory.

title: Wikipedia, Scope creep [anti-pattern]
text:
## Scope creep (anti-pattern)
Scope creep is continuous or uncontrolled growth in a project's scope, generally experienced after the project begins. It is a classic project and requirements failure mode that drives cost and schedule overruns and, in the worst case, outright project failure.

## Causes
Poor scope definition and ineffective communication between the client and the project manager produce misaligned expectations. Incomplete requirements capture, failing to gather information from all stakeholders during planning, leaves gaps that later surface as new work. Vague documentation, whether missing critical detail or too technical to be understood, invites reinterpretation. A low perceived cost of change lets small changes accumulate despite real complexity. Unnecessary feature additions, sometimes added just to impress the client, expand the boundary. Communication gaps and delayed stakeholder responses create bottlenecks that get filled with assumptions.

## Control through requirements management
Properly defining project scope requires thorough investigation and documents that clearly define what the project's scope is, what the goals are, and the methods for changing the scope. This is the requirements baseline: an agreed reference against which every proposed change is measured through a change control process. For a business analyst, scope creep is prevented not by refusing all change but by making change visible: a baselined set of requirements, an explicit change control procedure, and traceability so the impact of each new request can be assessed before it is accepted.

title: Lean Enterprise Institute, Value Stream Mapping
text:
## Value stream
A value stream is all the actions, both value creating and non value creating, required to bring a product from raw material to the arms of the customer. Thinking in value streams forces the analyst to look at the whole flow end to end, not at isolated departments or steps.

## Value stream mapping
Value stream mapping is diagramming every step involved in the material and information flows needed to bring a product from order to delivery. Unlike a plain process map, it captures both the material flow (the work moving through) and the information flow (the signals that trigger each step), which is why it exposes delays and handoffs that a single flowchart hides.

## Current state and future state
Teams typically begin by drawing a current state map that captures actual conditions as they are today, warts and all. Then they draw a future state map: a target image of how material and information should flow through the value stream. The gap between the two maps becomes the improvement plan.

## Purpose
Value stream mapping is a fundamental tool used in continuous improvement to identify and eliminate waste. It helps distinguish value creating steps from non value adding steps (waste), revealing where inventory piles up, where work waits, and where information is missing. For a business analyst doing process analysis, the value stream map is the artifact that turns a vague as is process into measurable evidence of where the real problems are, before anyone proposes a solution.

title: Wikipedia, Non-functional requirement
text:
## Functional versus non-functional
A functional requirement specifies what a system should do, typically phrased as system shall do requirement. A non-functional requirement (NFR) specifies how a system should be, an overall property of the system as a whole or of a particular aspect, typically phrased as system shall be requirement. Functional requirements define behavior; non-functional requirements constrain or judge that behavior.

## Quality attributes and the -ilities
Non-functional requirements are commonly known as the quality attributes of a system, and informally as the -ilities, from names like stability, portability, and maintainability. They split into two broad kinds. Execution qualities are observable while the system runs, such as safety, security, and usability. Evolution qualities are embodied in the static structure of the system, such as testability, maintainability, extensibility, and scalability.

## Common NFR categories
Widely used non-functional requirement types include performance and response time, throughput, scalability, capacity, availability, reliability, maintainability, safety, security, usability, accessibility, portability, testability, extensibility, and compliance. Because these attributes are easy to state vaguely (fast, secure, user friendly) and hard to verify, a top business analyst always turns each NFR into a measurable acceptance criterion: a specific target, a scale, and a condition of measurement (for example, 95 percent of page loads complete within 2 seconds under a stated load), rather than an adjective. Unmeasured non-functional requirements are the most common silent cause of a system that meets its functional spec yet is rejected in production.

title: Dan North, Introducing BDD
text:
## From testing to behaviour
Dan North developed Behaviour-Driven Development (BDD) because the word test in Test-Driven Development created confusion. He found the shift from thinking in tests to thinking in behaviour so profound that he started to refer to TDD as BDD. The reframe matters for a business analyst: you are not writing tests, you are specifying behaviour in language the business can read.

## Test names as should sentences
A test method name should read as a sentence, and North's convention is that it starts with should: the class should do something. The tool agiledox converted camelCase method names into readable sentences. If a method name does not fit the should pattern, it hints that the behaviour belongs somewhere else, which nudges better design and clearer requirements.

## Given, When, Then
North standardized the template for a scenario as: Given some initial context (the givens), When an event occurs, Then ensure some outcomes. This structure breaks a requirement into testable fragments that can be automated and reused across scenarios. It is the origin of the Given-When-Then form now used across BDD tools.

## User story template
Stories capture value explicitly with the template: As a [X] I want [Y] so that [Z]. Forcing the so that clause makes the team name the business value of the story at definition time, not after it is built.

## Executable acceptance criteria
North's vision is that acceptance criteria are directly executable: the given, when, then scenarios become end to end functional tests that bridge business language and technical implementation. Acceptance criteria are not an afterthought; they are the specification, written before the work and used to prove it is done.

title: Wikipedia, Five whys (root cause analysis)
text:
## What the Five Whys is
The Five Whys is an iterative interrogative technique used to explore the cause and effect relationships underlying a particular problem. You ask why about a problem, then ask why again about that answer, typically about five times, to move from the visible symptom to the root cause. It is a core tool for the business analyst doing problem analysis before proposing any solution.

## Origin
The technique was developed by Sakichi Toyoda and implemented within Toyota Motor Corporation. Taiichi Ohno, architect of the Toyota Production System, described it as the basis of Toyota's scientific approach to problem solving: repeat why five times and the nature of the problem as well as its solution becomes clear.

## Classic example
Starting from bolts that cross thread on a production line: why, the threads are not cut cleanly; why, the lathe cutting tool was not replaced; why, the replacement tool bin was empty; why, the bin contents fell under the shelves; why, a shelf foot rusted and failed, causing instability. The root cause is the broken shelf foot, so the countermeasure is a regular shelf inspection process, not merely re cutting the bolt.

## The point and its limits
The goal is to trace the chain of causality in direct increments from the effect, through any layers of abstraction, to a root cause that can be addressed so the problem does not recur. Known limitations: investigators often stop at symptoms rather than a true root cause; results are not repeatable across different analysts; the arbitrary fifth why may not be the real root cause; and the method tends to isolate a single cause when several may combine. A skilled analyst uses it alongside a fishbone (Ishikawa) cause and effect diagram when causes are multiple.

title: Suzanne and James Robertson, Volere Requirements Specification Template
text:
## The requirements shell (snow card)
The Volere template captures each requirement as an atomic requirement on a requirements shell, informally called a snow card. The shell is a guide to writing each atomic functional and non-functional requirement, and it forces completeness and traceability by structuring every requirement with the same attributes.

## Attributes of an atomic requirement
Each requirement carries: requirement number, description, rationale (why the requirement matters), source (who raised it), fit criterion, customer satisfaction and customer dissatisfaction ratings, priority, conflicts (other requirements it clashes with), supporting materials, and history. Recording rationale and source is what lets a BA later challenge a requirement that no longer has an owner or a reason.

## The fit criterion
The fit criterion is Volere's most important idea. It is a measurement that quantifies a requirement so it can be tested. A vague requirement such as the product shall be easy for 11 year old children to use is not testable. Its fit criterion makes it measurable: eighty percent of a test panel of 11 year old children shall be able to successfully complete a listed set of tasks within a specified time. Every requirement, functional or non-functional, gets a fit criterion, and that is how you guarantee verifiability.

## Functional versus non-functional
Functional requirements are the fundamental or essential subject matter of the product: they describe what the product has to do or what processing actions it is to take. Non-functional requirements describe the properties that those functions must have, such as performance and usability. The Volere shell treats both the same way: describe it, then attach a fit criterion so it can be verified.

title: Beck et al., Principles behind the Agile Manifesto
text:
## Principles behind the Agile Manifesto
The twelve principles frame how agile teams treat requirements, and a modern business analyst works inside them.
1. Our highest priority is to satisfy the customer through early and continuous delivery of valuable software.
2. Welcome changing requirements, even late in development. Agile processes harness change for the customer's competitive advantage.
3. Deliver working software frequently, from a couple of weeks to a couple of months, with a preference to the shorter timescale.
4. Business people and developers must work together daily throughout the project.
5. Build projects around motivated individuals. Give them the environment and support they need, and trust them to get the job done.
6. The most efficient and effective method of conveying information to and within a development team is face to face conversation.
7. Working software is the primary measure of progress.
8. Agile processes promote sustainable development. The sponsors, developers, and users should be able to maintain a constant pace indefinitely.
9. Continuous attention to technical excellence and good design enhances agility.
10. Simplicity, the art of maximizing the amount of work not done, is essential.
11. The best architectures, requirements, and designs emerge from self organizing teams.
12. At regular intervals, the team reflects on how to become more effective, then tunes and adjusts its behavior accordingly.

## Why this matters for a BA
Principle 2 (welcome changing requirements) and principle 4 (business and developers together daily) reframe the analyst from a document writer into a continuous conversation facilitator. Principle 10 (maximize work not done) is the direct antidote to gold plating and big requirements up front: the best requirement is often the feature you decide not to build.

title: Martin Fowler, SpecificationByExample
text:
## Specification by example
Specification by example describes requirements using concrete examples rather than abstract statements. Instead of writing a broad specification that tries to cover every case in theory, the team specifies behaviour through particular examples that stakeholders can easily understand and validate.

## Why examples beat abstractions
Fowler contrasts this with formal methods that rely on pre and post conditions, noting that examples are usually much easier to come up with, particularly for the non technical people we write the software for. A concrete example (given this input and this state, expect this result) is unambiguous in a way an abstract statement rarely is, and a business person can confirm or correct it immediately.

## Say it twice: the double check
The approach gains reliability by expressing intent twice, once in the code and once in the tests (the examples). Because the two are written in distinct ways, a mismatch between them surfaces an error. This is the same discipline as writing acceptance criteria as executable given, when, then scenarios.

## Limits and collaboration
Fowler is explicit that examples cannot stand alone: tests are always going to be incomplete, so they always have to be backed up with other mechanisms. And the technique only works in the context of a working relationship where both sides are collaborating and not fighting. The examples trigger abstractions in the design team while keeping those abstractions grounded in real cases. For a business analyst, the practical rule is: whenever a requirement feels ambiguous, ask for a concrete example, and then another, until the rule is clear.

title: Wikipedia, Kano model (customer satisfaction and requirement prioritization)
text:
## The Kano model
The Kano model is a product development and customer satisfaction theory developed in the 1980s by Noriaki Kano. It classifies product features by how their presence or absence affects customer satisfaction, which makes it a powerful prioritization lens for a business analyst deciding which requirements matter most.

## The five categories
Must-be quality (Basic or Threshold): requirements customers expect as a baseline. When done well, customers are just neutral; when done poorly, customers are very dissatisfied. Examples: working brakes in a car, a clean hotel room. These are the requirements nobody thanks you for but everyone punishes you for missing.
One-dimensional quality (Performance or Linear): features that create satisfaction when present and dissatisfaction when absent, in proportion to how much is delivered. These are the competitive differentiators customers actively discuss, like acceleration or resolution time.
Attractive quality (Excitement or Delighters): unexpected features that delight when included but do not disappoint when absent. They provide satisfaction when achieved fully but do not cause dissatisfaction when not fulfilled.
Indifferent quality: aspects that neither satisfy nor dissatisfy; candidates to cut to reduce cost.
Reverse quality: features whose presence actually dissatisfies some customers, because preferences differ (some want minimalism, some want everything).

## Satisfaction dynamics
Categories shift over time as competitive standards evolve: today's delighter becomes tomorrow's basic expectation. The BA lesson: prioritize Must-be requirements first (they are non negotiable), invest in the One-dimensional features that differentiate, add a few Attractive delighters, and stop spending on Indifferent ones. Do not assume a feature stays exciting forever.

title: Business Analyst Mentor, Problem Analysis [anti-pattern: solutioning first]
text:
## Understand the problem before the solution
The goal of problem analysis is to gain a better understanding of the problem being solved before developing a solution. The classic business analysis anti-pattern is jumping directly to a solution without this groundwork, which leads to flawed approaches. Clients rarely bring a problem; they bring an assumption disguised as a solution. If you reach the answer before agreeing on the question, you cannot know you are solving the right problem.

## Symptoms versus root causes
A key pitfall is treating surface level issues as if they were the fundamental problem. Root cause analysis helps prevent the development of solutions that are focused on symptoms alone. Distinguishing symptoms from underlying causes, and needs from wants, is essential to avoid misdirected effort. By understanding the real world problem and the user's actual needs, you determine better solutions that address those needs rather than the first idea someone voiced.

## The five step framework
1. Gain agreement on the problem definition, formalized as a written problem statement. 2. Understand root causes, the problem behind the problem, using techniques like fishbone diagrams or the 5 Whys. 3. Identify the stakeholders and users, because solving a complex problem typically means satisfying the needs of a diverse group. 4. Define the solution boundary, establishing scope. 5. Identify constraints, considering economic, environmental, technical, and political restrictions.

## Problem statement template
Use a standardized problem statement: the problem of [description] affects [stakeholders], the impact of which is [impact], and a successful solution would [benefits of proposed solution]. Writing the problem down in this form, before any design, is the single most reliable guard against solutioning.

title: Techcanvass, Types of Requirements as per BABOK (Requirements Classification Schema)
text:
## BABOK requirements classification schema
The BABOK Guide classifies requirements into four levels, and knowing which level you are working at prevents a common error: answering a solution question when the business goal has never been agreed.

## Business requirements
Statements of goals, objectives, and outcomes that describe why a change has been initiated. They can apply to the whole of an enterprise, a business area, or a specific initiative. Example: automate the customer relationship management system to improve response time by 70 percent within 6 months. Business requirements answer why.

## Stakeholder requirements
Describe the needs of stakeholders that must be met in order to achieve the business requirements. They bridge the high level business requirements and the detailed solution requirements. Example: implement daily monitoring of customer support response times with reports available on demand or scheduled, including comparative trend analysis.

## Solution requirements
The most detailed level, split into two subtypes. Functional requirements: the features and functions the system must perform (for example user registration, online purchasing); they define what the system must do. Non-functional requirements (quality of service): quality attributes and environmental conditions such as accessibility, safety, performance, scalability, and reusability; for example every page should load in 5 seconds.

## Transition requirements
Describe the capabilities the solution must have and the conditions it must meet to facilitate transition from the current state to the future state, but which are not needed once the change is complete. Examples: user training programs and migrating historical data to the new system. Transition requirements are temporary by definition, which is why they are tracked separately from the ongoing solution requirements.

title: Martin Fowler, UbiquitousLanguage (Domain-Driven Design)
text:
## Ubiquitous Language
Ubiquitous Language, articulated by Eric Evans in Domain-Driven Design, is a rigorous, shared vocabulary between software developers and domain experts, rooted in the domain model used in the software itself. The same terms are used in conversation, in the model, and in the code, and the language evolves as the team's understanding deepens. For a business analyst, this is the discipline that keeps requirements from meaning different things to different readers.

## Why it matters
Evans emphasizes that software does not cope well with ambiguity, so a precise shared language is necessary. Using the ubiquitous language in conversations with domain experts is itself a validation method: it tests both the language and the underlying domain model. When developers and domain experts use different words for the same concept, or the same word for different concepts, defects follow.

## Mutual accountability
Evans's rule: domain experts should object to terms or structures that are awkward or inadequate to convey domain understanding, and developers should watch for ambiguity or inconsistency that will trip up design. Both sides police the language. By consistently applying a model based language and refining it until it flows naturally, teams develop models that are complete and comprehensible, made of simple elements that combine to express complex ideas. A glossary of agreed domain terms is one of the highest leverage artifacts a BA can maintain.

title: Jama Software, Requirements Traceability (Requirements Management Guide)
text:
## What requirements traceability is
Requirements traceability is the practice of linking requirements throughout the product development lifecycle, from their origin through development, testing, and final release. It creates connections between different development artifacts so a team can see how each requirement is fulfilled and what the impact of a change would be.

## Bidirectional traceability
Traceability is bidirectional. Backward traceability links a requirement to its source, the business requirement, stakeholder, or regulation it came from, so you can ask why does this requirement exist. Forward traceability links a requirement to the design specifications, code, and test cases that implement and verify it, so you can ask is this requirement built and proven. Following the chain in both directions is what makes change safe.

## The requirements traceability matrix
The requirements traceability matrix (RTM) is the core tool: it maps each requirement to its related artifacts, especially the test cases and design specifications that satisfy it. The RTM makes coverage visible: every requirement should trace forward to at least one test, and every test should trace back to a requirement, so you catch both untested requirements and orphan tests.

## Why it matters
Traceability provides proof of requirement coverage, which is essential for demonstrating compliance with industry regulations. It reduces development risk by exposing the impact of a change early: if a stakeholder asks to alter one requirement, the trace shows every design element, code module, and test that the change touches. That impact analysis is the difference between a controlled change and scope creep, and it is why traceability, not just a tidy document, is a core business analysis discipline.

title: iSixSigma, SIPOC Diagram
text:
## SIPOC
SIPOC is an acronym for Supplier, Input, Process, Output, Customer. It is a high level process map used in Six Sigma, most often in the Define phase of DMAIC, to agree the scope and boundaries of a process before anyone dives into detail. On one page it answers who supplies what, what the process does, and who receives the result.

## The five columns
Supplier: the entity that provides input or inputs to a process. Input: all that is used, mostly as variables, to produce one or more outputs from a process. Process: the steps or activities carried out to convert inputs to one or more outputs; in a SIPOC the process steps are shown at a high level, typically four to seven steps. Output: one or more outcomes or physical products emerging from a process. Customer: the entity that uses the output or outputs of a process.

## How it is used
A SIPOC deliberately stays high level so a team and its sponsor can align on scope fast and spot the suppliers and customers who must be involved in the analysis. It is the natural precursor to a detailed process model (a swimlane or value stream map): first agree the boundary and the players with SIPOC, then model the internal steps. For a business analyst, SIPOC is the fastest way to prevent the argument where two stakeholders think the project covers different things, because the process boundary and its inputs and outputs are made explicit and agreed on one sheet.

title: Wikipedia, Data-flow diagram
text:
## What a data flow diagram is
A data flow diagram (DFD) is a way of representing the flow of data through a process or a system, usually an information system. It shows how information moves through the organization's processes and where it is stored, deliberately without control flow, decision logic, or loops (those belong in a flowchart or BPMN model, not a DFD). It answers what data is used and produced, not the order of steps.

## The four components
Process (also called function or transformation): drawn as a circle, oval, or rounded rectangle; it transforms inputs into outputs. Data flow: drawn as a labeled arrow showing the transfer of information (sometimes material) from one part of the system to another; the label names the data that moves. Data store (warehouse): drawn as two parallel horizontal lines; it retains information for later retrieval, such as a database, filing system, or document folder. Terminator (external entity): an external source or sink of data such as an organization, a customer group, or an external department that sits outside the modeled system.

## Notations and leveling
Two common notations exist: Yourdon and DeMarco (described in 1979) and Gane and Sarson. DFDs are drawn in levels of increasing detail. The context diagram (level 0 in some conventions) shows the entire system as a single process with its external entities and the data that crosses the boundary. Decomposing that single process yields a level 1 diagram with numbered processes (1, 2, 3), and each of those can be exploded again into level 2 (1.1, 1.2, 1.3), so detail is added without losing the big picture. This leveling discipline is why DFDs remain a useful requirements and analysis tool for data intensive systems.

title: Ron Jeffries, Essential XP: Card, Conversation, Confirmation
text:
## The three C's
Ron Jeffries coined the three C's that define what a user story really is: Card, Conversation, Confirmation. This is the single most important corrective to the mistake of treating a written story as a complete specification.

## Card
The card does not contain all the information that makes up the requirement. Instead, the card has just enough text to identify the requirement and to remind everyone what the story is. The card is a token representing the requirement, not the requirement itself. It is a placeholder, a promise for a conversation.

## Conversation
The requirement itself is communicated from customer to programmers through conversation: an exchange of thoughts, opinions, and feelings. This discussion happens during estimation and iteration planning, and examples are the most effective supplement to it. The detail lives in the conversation, not on the card, which is why a business analyst's job is to facilitate and capture that conversation, not to write ever longer cards.

## Confirmation
At the beginning of the iteration, the customer communicates to the programmers what she wants by telling them how she will confirm that they have done what is needed. Acceptance tests provide that concrete verification. The confirmation provided by the acceptance test is what makes possible the simple approach of card and conversation: because you agreed up front how you would prove the story is done, you can safely defer the rest of the detail. A story without confirmation (acceptance criteria) is not ready.

title: Martin Fowler, BusinessReadableDSL
text:
## Business readable, not business writeable
Martin Fowler argues that the primary value of a domain specific language for specifications and rules is not that business people write it, but that they can read it. The sweet spot is in making DSLs business readable rather than business writeable. This directly explains why Gherkin and given, when, then scenarios are valuable to a business analyst: their point is that a stakeholder can read the specification and confirm it, not that the stakeholder authors the automation.

## The communication channel
If business people are able to look at the DSL code and understand it, then we can build a deep and rich communication channel between software development and the underlying domain. In Fowler's model, programmers write the code but show that code frequently to business people who can understand what it means; these customers can then make changes, maybe draft some code, but it is the programmers who make it solid and do the debugging and testing. The requirement is validated by the business reading it in their own language.

## A caution on writeable DSLs
Fowler warns that making a DSL business writeable is expensive, because you must build proper tooling: editors, error messages, debugging. He invokes COBOL's failure to eliminate programmers as a historical lesson, with spreadsheets as a notable exception. The BA takeaway: invest in specifications the business can read and confirm (acceptance criteria, examples, readable scenarios), and do not chase the fantasy that non technical stakeholders will maintain executable rules themselves.
